citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The attending veterinarian’s site visits have not been performed at the frequency agreed upon in the written Program of
Veterinary Care. The current Program of Veterinary Care states the attending veterinarian will have regularly scheduled
visits bi-annually. The attending veterinarian was consulted and stated that bi-annually meant a frequency of once every 6
months. The last veterinary visit to the facility, per the attending veterinarian, was on October 5, 2025.
Not following the prescribed frequency of regularly scheduled veterinary premises visits can lead to an inadequate
standard of veterinary care for the animals. The licensee shall ensure the correct frequency of regularly scheduled
attending veterinarian visits occurs as prescribed in the written Program of Veterinary Care.
Correct by: 11/01/2026

citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility’s methods to control and prevent diseases were inadequate. The licensee is not following the vaccine protocol
as described in the Program of Veterinary Care approved by the attending veterinarian. Per the Program of Veterinary
Care, cats should be given rabies and distemper once every 12 months and goats and sheep should receive rabies once
every 12 months as well.
At the time of the inspection, only five cats had received their rabies vaccine out of the eleven housed at the facility per
veterinary records. In addition, there is no veterinary record of any ruminants receiving rabies vaccine. Upon interview, the
attending veterinarian stated that both rabies and distemper vaccines should be given as documented in the program of
vet care. Failing to follow the agreed upon vaccine schedule does not prevent the potential transmission of disease
hazards.
Facilities must use appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose and treat disease and injuries. The facility needs to
follow the instructions provided by the attending veterinarian and as directed in the written program of veterinary care.

The unsealed wood in the cat room needs to be addressed. The facility moved the cats into the old lemur holding area.
The wood along the walls and door frame still had evidence of lemur scent marking grime and debris. The licensee states
that the material coming off was the sealant that covered the wood. When wood is no longer sealed and impervious to
moisture, then these interior surfaces can no longer be readily cleaned and sanitized. Interior surfaces for cats must be
able to be cleaned and sanitized to facilitate cleaning of the area and to reduce disease hazards.
The surfaces of cat housing facilities - including houses, dens, and other furniture-type fixtures and objects within the
facility - must be constructed in a manner and made of materials that allow them to be readily cleaned and sanitized or
removed or replaced when worn or soiled.
Correct by: 10/15/2026

The metal bed frame with a wood platform is in disrepair in the kangaroo enclosure. This provided furniture is available for
the kangaroos to rest on off the ground but has a large hole in the wood that has sharp edges that could potentially cause
harm to the kangaroos.
This provided furniture must be constructed of such material and of such strength as appropriate for the animals involved
and shall be maintained in good repair to protect the animals from injury.
Correct by: 10/12/2026

The outdoor enclosure for one armadillo did not have adequate drainage. One half of the enclosure was a thick layer of
mud, and the other half had standing water over the concrete floor approximately 1-2 inches deep. The armadillo was
found in the back of its shelter, a plastic doghouse structure, the only dry area within its enclosure. Its water and food bowl
were present on the concrete portion of the enclosure which would require the armadillo to walk through both the mud and
standing water to reach them.
Enclosures that do not drain effectively and in which the ground is muddy with no dry path to their food, water, or shelter,
can cause animals to develop foot or skin issues due to excessive moisture and mud exposure or cause discomfort.
The licensee must provide a suitable method to rapidly eliminate excess water or otherwise prevent the situation where
the animals have no dry surfaces on which to walk to reach their food, water, and/or shelter.
Correct by: 10/10/2026

Pest control at the facility needs to be addressed. An effective program is not being maintained to reduce rodents in the
feed room or flies in the animal encounter room.
The feed room had evidence of one rodent bait box but did not seem to be effective in reducing the entry of rodents into
the area. Rodent droppings were present on the lids of almost every food container around the room.
No fly mitigation practices were observed to be in effect in the animal encounter room and there was an abundance of
flies around the hedgehogs, including dead flies in their clean water bowl.
For the animals’ welfare and to protect the food supplies, a safe and effective program for the control of insects, and
mammalian pests shall be established and maintained at the facility.
Correct by: 10/12/2026
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the licensee.
